subject: Cloud Computing
title: Time-Sharing: Computing by the Hour
description: A quick, practical guide to Time-Sharing: Computing by the Hour.

hook.text: Computers in the 1960s cost millions. An MIT professor had a radical idea: share the cost.

buildup.text: John McCarthy proposed time-sharing — one computer slicing its time among many users.

discovery.text: Each user got a tiny slice of processing time, but it felt like they had the whole machine.

twist.text: Time-sharing companies sold computing by the hour. They were the first cloud providers.

climax.text: The industry crashed in the 1980s when personal computers made shared access seem pointless.

punchline.text: Cheap PCs killed time-sharing. Then the internet revived it.

quiz.question: Why did the original time-sharing industry decline in the 1980s?
options: Personal computers became affordable, reducing need for shared access
Time-sharing was made illegal by the government
The internet replaced all time-sharing companies directly

details.summary: Time-sharing systems in the 1960s allowed multiple users to use a computer simultaneously, each getting a slice of processing time. Companies even sold computing time by the hour, creating the earliest version of the pay-as-you-go model cloud providers use today.
details.whyItMatters: Time-sharing established the economic model for cloud computing: rent computing power by usage instead of owning hardware. This shift from ownership to access defines the cloud era.
takeaways: Time-sharing gave each user a slice of processing time
Computing was sold by the hour, like modern cloud billing
It introduced the rent-not-own model for computing

faq.question: How did time-sharing differ from batch processing?
faq.answer: Batch processing ran jobs sequentially with no user interaction. Time-sharing rapidly switched between users, giving each one an interactive experience. Users felt like they had the computer to themselves, even though they were sharing it with dozens of others.

faq.question: Who predicted utility computing?
faq.answer: John McCarthy suggested in 1961 that computing might be sold as a utility like electricity. This vision took decades to realize, but modern cloud computing fulfills exactly his prediction: computing power available on demand, billed by consumption.
